title: Ephemeral canary shields: SDK authz + snapshot-rewind for safe auto-rollback
creator: Ava Patel
description: Add SDK and API primitives that let clients create short-lived, least-privilege canary tokens ("ephemeral shields") which: 1) are scoped to a single canary experiment or A/B slice, 2) include idempotency and replay protection metadata, and 3) are tied to a lightweight snapshot checkpoint used by the control plane to implement fast auto-rollback ("snapshot-rewind"). This ticket covers API surface, client helpers, permission model, tracing hooks, and rollback activation flow. The goal is to reduce blast radius for canaries, make rollouts auditable and replay-safe, and enable sub-minute automatic rollback that restores previous inference routing and cache state consistency.
acceptance_criteria: API: POST /v1/rollouts/{id}/ephemeral-tokens creates a token with scope, ttl, and idempotency key and returns token metadata and token_id.
SDK: client helper issues ephemeral shields and transparently attaches token metadata to requests; helper exposes refresh(), revoke() and tokenInfo() calls.
AuthZ: token grants are scoped to route/model/version/canary_id and cannot be elevated by client SDK; control plane validates scope server-side.
Snapshot-rewind: control plane stores a compact snapshot reference at token issuance that can be used to rewind routing and KV cache pointers when an auto-rollback triggers.
Observability: every ephemeral token lifecycle event emits structured traces and audit log entries (issue, refresh, revoke, expired, used-by-request).
Idempotency: duplicate token creation with same client-supplied idempotency key returns the original token metadata (idempotent create).
Security: security review signoff obtained and token format passes threat modelling for replay and leakage scenarios.
implementation_plan: Design API contract and OpenAPI schema for ephemeral token endpoints (create, revoke, introspect).
Design SDK surface: EphemeralTokenManager in JS/Python with createToken(), attachToRequest(), autoRefresh(), and revoke().
Backend: lightweight token service stores token metadata and snapshot reference; tokens are opaque JWT-like but signed by control-plane key and validated on edge.
Control-plane hooks: on token create, persist snapshot pointer to routing + KV cache checkpoint; expose rollback operation that uses snapshot pointer.
Edge validation: modify ingress to accept token header X-Rollout-Token, validate signature and scope, and annotate request with canary metadata for routing.
Tracing/audit: emit events to telemetry pipeline and append to audit log; surface in Console rollouts UI.
E2E tests: simulate canary that introduces regression, trigger auto-rollback, verify routing and cache state return to pre-canary snapshot.
technical_considerations: Token format trade-offs: opaque db-backed tokens allow immediate revoke but require lookup; self-contained signed tokens reduce DB reads but complicate revoke semantics. Plan: short-lived signed tokens (TTL 5-15m) + optional revocation table for manual revoke.

Snapshot granularity: full KV cache snapshot is heavy; use routing + KV index pointers and a compact cache-warmup plan. Rewind will restore routing table and schedule async cache warmup to avoid cold starts.
Idempotency model: use client-supplied idempotency-key with server-side dedup window aligned to token TTL. Expired entries garbage-collected.

Permissions: ensure token-scoped policy enforced server-side; do not trust client-specified model/version claims without control-plane validation. Map ephemeral token to existing RBAC roles for auditing.
Replay protection: embed issued_at + nonce in token signature; edges check nonce uniqueness in short window to detect reuse from replayed network captures.
Performance: token validation should be O(1) and on hot path; prefer signature verification cached per edge pod. DB lookups only for rare revocations.
Compatibility: make SDK helpers optionally pluggable into existing route-based rollout clients; backward compatibility with current routing header approach.
risk_and_mitigation: Risk: Token leakage could allow attacker to target canary slices. Mitigation: very short TTLs, replay nonce, strict scope binding, and ability to revoke tokens immediately via control plane.

Risk: Snapshot-rewind might lead to inconsistent cache state if not carefully coordinated. Mitigation: restore routing pointers synchronously, schedule cache warmup tasks, and use traffic draining for in-flight requests.
Risk: Increased latency from token validation. Mitigation: cache validation results at edge and use lightweight signature scheme.
